title: Mighty Babylon Will Fall
overview: Jeremiah announces that Babylon, the empire that crushed Judah, will itself be conquered, while the scattered people of Israel and Judah come home and are forgiven.

parts.label: Babylon's gods disgraced (vv. 1-3)
parts.note: Bel, a title meaning 'lord', and Marduk both name Babylon's chief god, pictured here as too terrified to protect his own city. The attacker from the north is usually identified as the Medes and Persians, whose king Cyrus took Babylon in 539 BC, though the total emptiness described came only gradually over later centuries.

parts.label: Lost sheep head home (vv. 4-10)
parts.note: Misled by their own leaders and preyed on by enemies who excused themselves by pointing to the people's own guilt, Israel and Judah return weeping to seek God and bind themselves to him in an everlasting covenant, a binding agreement. They are urged to leave Babylon quickly, like the male goats that walk at the front of a flock.

parts.label: Payback for the plunderer (vv. 11-16)
parts.note: Babylon gloated as it looted God's people, frisking like a well fed animal, so now archers are told to do to her what she did to others. Even her farmers will be cut off, and the many peoples Babylon had deported will scatter back to their homelands.

parts.label: A mauled flock forgiven (vv. 17-20)
parts.note: Israel is pictured as a sheep attacked first by Assyria and then by Babylon's king Nebuchadnezzar, and God promises to punish Babylon as he did Assyria and return his people to rich grazing land. Their guilt will be searched for and not found because God forgives those he spares, which Christians read alongside the new covenant they see fulfilled in Jesus.

parts.label: The hammer of the earth broken (vv. 21-32)
parts.note: Merathaim and Pekod were real places in Babylonia, but their names also sound like Hebrew words for 'double rebellion' and 'punishment', a grim pun. The commands to kill and destroy are stark, and the text presents them as repayment for Babylon's pride and for destroying God's temple in Jerusalem.

parts.label: The Redeemer's sword (vv. 33-46)
parts.note: A redeemer was a close relative bound to buy family members back from slavery, and God takes that role for captives whose masters will not release them, bringing a sword on Babylon until it lies empty like Sodom. The army from the north and the lion from the Jordan repeat words used earlier in Jeremiah against Jerusalem and Edom, now turned on Babylon itself.

disagreement: Christians differ on whether the promises of return and complete forgiveness were fulfilled in the Jewish return from exile, are fulfilled spiritually in Jesus and the church, or still await a future restoration of Israel.
think: When people crushed by a powerful empire long for its total ruin, how do you weigh their cry for justice against the suffering that ruin would bring to ordinary people living inside that empire?
